title_original: Doc Talk At Doc Stories: Podcast Encounters Festival Leaders Anne Lai & Jessie Fairbanks, Filmmakers Sam Pollard, J.M. Harper

blocks.text: Many of documentary’s leading lights gathered in San Francisco this month for Doc Stories, the prestigious four-day festival put on by SFFilm. Oscar winner Laura Poitras, two-time Oscar winner Ben Proudfoot, Oscar nominees Ava DuVernay and Sam Pollard, Sundance directing award winner J.M. Harper and more came to the City by the Bay for what has emerged as an increasingly important event on the nonfiction film calendar.

For a third year in a row, Deadline’s Doc Talk podcast joined the festivities. On the latest edition of the pod, we visit with Anne Lai, executive director of SFFilm, and director of programming Jessie Fairbanks for a conversation about the 12th edition of Doc Stories. The festival leaders tell us why they limit the event to a tightly curated lineup of 10 features and two shorts blocs. We also get into the breakout success of the Elizabeth Holmes-focused documentary You Can See Everything and whether it will be embraced by Oscar documentary branch voters, who sometimes sniff at stylistic innovations such as those deployed in Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s film. Lai tells us why she likens the doc branch to the Electoral College — an institution noted for its power to upend the popular vote.

blocks.text: We also spend time with Pollard to explore his Oscar-contending documentary Tutu , about the late Archbishop Desmond Tutu, who won the Nobel Peace Prize for helping to bring down South Africa’s racist system of apartheid. As his film documents, President Nelson Mandela handed an exceedingly difficult task to the archbishop after white rule fell – leading a Truth and Reconciliation Commission to come to terms with South Africa’s long and brutal history of strict racial segregation. Pollard tells us why he believes the U.S. will never have its own Truth and Reconciliation Commission.

Harper joins Doc Talk along with Pollard, discussing his award-winning documentary Soul Patrol that examines a super-elite all-Black unit in the Vietnam War. At the age of 14, Harper became fascinated by the war, even though it had long since ended by the time he was born. The filmmaker explains why the war has absorbed his focus for so many years, and how his documentary grew out of reading the memoir Soul Patrol , written by Vietnam veteran Ed Emanuel.

That’s on the new episode of Doc Talk hosted by Oscar winner John Ridley ( 12 Years a Slave , Shirley ) and Matt Carey, Deadline’s senior documentary editor. The pod is a production of Deadline and Ridley’s Nō Studios.
